---
# A Defense of Getting Lost

There was a time, not so long ago, when a wrong turn could stretch across an afternoon. You were on a country road with a paper map folded open on the passenger seat, and a turn you should have taken passed in a silver blur. By the time you admitted it, the scenery had become entirely unfamiliar. The road narrowed, cattle watched from fields, and a town appeared with a name you had never seen. For the next hour, every junction became a question. Gas stations offered hints. A mechanic drew a route on a napkin. Eventually you found the highway, but the mistake remained lodged in memory longer than the destination, a small adventure whose details sharpened whenever someone asked, “What happened when you get lost?”

My first serious geography was learned at the scale of a summer vacation. We had two paper maps: one for driving and one for walking, though neither was designed for children. Before leaving, I taped them to the kitchen table and traced routes with my finger, inventing detours through towns whose names sounded like ingredients in an unfamiliar recipe. Borders seemed less like lines than like doors. Rivers had the dignity of roads. I did not know then that the blank regions of the map—the pale spaces between printed names—were invitations, or at least felt that way. I thought a person could step off the edge of the known world and discover something arranged with equal care but for a different audience.

Then came the blue dot. It glowed patiently in the corner of a phone, a tiny moon assuring us that the world was knowable. Turn left in four hundred feet. Merge onto the motorway. Continue straight. The route recalculated when we made a mistake, its calm voice restoring order before uncertainty had time to become an experience. Convenience was real, and I am grateful for it. A nurse on a winter road, a family carrying too much luggage, a traveler with a broken-down car: navigation technology can be a kind of mercy. But the same system gives our attention a narrow assignment. We are told where to look, and because looking is so expensive, we stop seeing much of what the route contains.

This is the bargain of efficient travel. The fastest route is treated as the best route, the measurable distance as the truest measure of a journey. A shortcut past a construction site beats the scenic road; a motorway bypasses the town center where the sign advertises hand-painted shoes; a station is not a place so much as a transfer point between addresses. The map remembers all of this, but the map has been instructed to forget. Yet the detour is often where a journey acquires texture. The missed exit introduces a new accent, a different architecture, a roadside produce stand, a dog asleep in a patch of sun. Efficiency compresses the road; uncertainty unfolds it.

Still, “getting lost” should not be confused with being lost. One is a temporary condition, often a form of play; the other can be an emergency. A hiker without water, a traveler in a neighborhood where the signs have changed, a person who cannot read the language around them: these are not picturesque predicaments. The point of defending lostness is not to make danger seem charming. It is to notice that perfect certainty has its own danger. It can make us careless, arrogant, and shallow. When every route is pre-chosen, we may arrive safely but have not necessarily gone anywhere except from one point to another.

What does lostness awaken? For a little while, the senses become newly accountable. You notice the slope of a street because your legs are tired. You notice smells because you cannot smell them by choice. You hear a gate closing somewhere behind a wall, a church bell, the particular percussion of a train crossing an iron bridge. A landmark that would have registered as scenery now becomes information: the blue awning, the statue with one hand missing, the bakery whose exhaust vents warm air onto the pavement. Attention is often described as a spotlight, but uncertainty feels more like opening the curtains. The ordinary world stops being background and becomes a text you are suddenly able, and compelled, to read.

Maps are compressed stories. Every map is an argument about what matters. It enlarges the capital, shrinks the marsh, smooths the mountain, straightens the river, and places a neat dot beside the place where you are standing. Even the familiar road atlas is selective in ways that feel natural until you examine it. Railways, boundaries, towns, rivers: some lines are bold, others nearly invisible. We accept this because maps are practical, but every simplification is also a tiny act of authorship. The blue line of a subway map may bend geometry so that stations can be read easily; a national map may make an entire region look like an afterthought. A map does not merely show the world. It interprets it, and in doing so teaches us what to overlook.

This is why wrong directions can be richer than right ones. “Take the road past the church, turn at the bridge with the red railings, then follow the smell of the bakery” contains weather, architecture, appetite, and memory. It assumes a human scale. It turns landmarks into a story and, unlike a list of street numbers, allows the traveler to become part of the place. Such directions are imperfect by design. They depend on what the speaker knows, what the listener notices, and what happens to be open. I once received directions to a house in a city I had visited only twice: “Go up the hill until you see the television antennas, then take the second stairway after the small white car.” I found the antennas, though not the car, and the stairway anyway. I have never located that house by those instructions since.

Walking restores sequence to space. From above, a neighborhood is a pattern; at street level, it is a succession of thresholds. You pass a shuttered kiosk, a doorway propped open with a crate, a tree growing through a fence, three chairs arranged for a conversation that has not yet begun. The pedestrian’s map is not mainly a network but a rhythm: curb, crossing, corner, pause, incline. Because you travel at the body’s speed, the neighborhood reveals itself in human doses. A two-block detour is not a rounding error on a screen; it is long enough to change your mood, to meet a dog, to understand why the main street bends. Distance measured in minutes by a car can be measured in stories by a walker.

To get lost deliberately, you do not need to wander into danger. You can begin with a rule: take the next street after the one you planned; leave the main road at the third traffic light; choose the path that appears least likely to contain what you want. On a walk, skip the café you already know. Sit on a bench facing a direction you cannot identify. On a train, get off one station early and walk home. The object is not confusion. It is the temporary loosening of the destination’s authority. The destination has a useful tyranny over us: it makes the route feel like mere space to be crossed. Once it loses absolute power, small possibilities become visible. A different street can become an afternoon; an unchosen platform can become a new city.

Another reward is humility. The navigable world can seem like a world that exists chiefly for our convenience, arranged around a central “I.” The blue dot confirms the ego with mechanical patience. Yet off-route, the center disperses. A street bears signs of lives we will never know. A demolished house leaves a rectangle of paler brick. Someone’s laundry moves in the breeze behind a glass door. The city stops presenting itself as a backdrop to our errands and becomes a dense field of other people. There is an ethical pleasure in that correction. It does not make the world fairer, but it makes our own scale less convincing, and that modest reduction in certainty can be a beginning of courtesy.

It also revives dialogue. Navigation apps have made asking for directions less common, and sometimes that is wonderfully practical; yet a request for help creates a brief, almost ceremonial exchange between strangers. We are not merely acquiring coordinates. We are asking another person to place us inside a local knowledge we do not possess. The answer may be detailed, vague, affectionate, contradictory. “You can’t miss it,” someone may say, and you both understand that you probably will. The directions become a tiny collaboration. In the process, the place acquires a human voice. It stops being an interface and becomes, for a minute, a shared thing.

There is a seasonal quality to this uncertainty, too. Some cities are hospitable to wandering; others seem to repel it. A neighborhood of broad roads and numbered blocks may be easy to cross but difficult to inhabit imaginatively. A tangle of small streets, courtyards, alleys, and passages can feel hostile on a map yet intimate in person. In one part of a city, every corner announces a business. In another, blank walls hide gardens, workshops, shrines, and courtyards where chairs are stacked for the evening. The same route may change character after a single turn. Navigation software does not always distinguish these places well, because its categories are functional: road, transit line, point of interest. Human attachment tends to be less orderly. It gathers around benches, smells, voices, and the particular door that looked as though it might belong to a secret.

Nature makes the case more sharply. A trail map often shows a line, a contour, a symbol for a spring, but the lived landscape is birdsong, damp stone, the angle of late light, the smell of resin, the fact that the path keeps disappearing behind a boulder even though the map insists it continues. Topographic maps are beautiful precisely because they translate sensory richness into signs without pretending the signs are the thing itself. Their blank spaces are not really blank. They are placeholders for lichen, weather, fatigue, and surprise. Walking through one does not mean rejecting the map; it means allowing the map to be joined by a world it cannot contain.

This also touches the question of borders. Political maps draw lines so sharply that landscapes can seem to end at them: the field on one side belongs to one flag, the field on the other to another, though the grass may cross without permission and the same bird may ignore the distinction. To travel through a border is to watch abstraction meet the ground. A line on a map can follow a river, a ridge, a road, or nothing visible at all. The walker feels how arbitrary official geometry can be and how stubborn physical geography can be. Getting lost, or choosing an unmarked path, restores the landscape’s continuity. It reminds us that authority is powerful partly because we are taught to see only its lines.

None of this means we should romanticize the pre-digital age. A paper map goes out of date; a train timetable loses its confidence; a neighborhood can change while the instructions remain the same. A driver reading directions at a busy intersection is not taking a contemplative detour. People get stranded, delayed, and frightened. Systems that reduce uncertainty have liberated many lives from burdens we should not sneer at. The defense I am making is not a demand that everyone should be inefficient. It is a request that efficiency not become the only atmosphere in which we move through the world. Convenience can be a tool; it should not be our philosophy of attention.

A practical way to defend some uncertainty is to make tiny rituals of it. Once a week, walk the long way through a familiar neighborhood. Take a book, leave the phone in a pocket, and navigate from signs, shadows, landmarks, and memory. On a trip, spend an hour in a district that has no item on your list. Learn the names of the streets near your home. Choose a train without checking its final destination. Ask someone how to get somewhere, then listen for the landmarks rather than converting every answer immediately into a pin on a map. These are not tests of toughness. They are ways of restoring the world’s grain, of feeling the difference between a place as a list of amenities and a place as a place.

Getting lost can also mean being lost among people, not only among streets. In a large city, a new arrival may have a dozen addresses, a map full of points, and still feel unable to locate the ordinary texture of belonging. The famous monument is easy; the corner where the fruit seller complains about the weather is not. Neighborhoods begin when repeated details become familiar: the dog that waits at the same gate, the laundrette open until nine, the bench that catches the last sun, the friend’s kitchen window. Until then, the city is an array of options without a rhythm. To wander without an efficient errand is sometimes how a place changes from background into home.

This is one reason so many travel stories are less about landmarks than about mistakes. The scheduled destination can be summarized in a sentence; the detour requires a story. You remember the closed road that sent you through a village during its festival. You remember the station café where a stranger corrected your pronunciation. You remember the night you missed the last bus, the borrowed room, the morning that revealed a town painted in colors you would never have seen at the required speed. These episodes are not valuable merely because they were inconvenient. They matter because they made us available to circumstance. A good journey does not merely carry us across a map. It changes the map inside us, adding rooms, voices, wrong turns, and the knowledge that there are more ways through than the route suggested.

And when we return, the place has changed too, though perhaps not in the ways we expected. The route home feels longer because the mind has enlarged with detours. Streets that once seemed interchangeable separate into distinct faces. A turn that used to be automatic becomes a decision. There is a strange pleasure in recognizing not the old instructions but the new landmarks: the bakery, the missing hand, the wall where the afternoon light falls. We have not become different people, exactly. Our attention has been stretched, and the ordinary world has been able to get inside it. That enlargement is not dramatic. It rarely arrives as revelation. More often it is a willingness to pause, a sharper sense of proportion, a morning when you look up and notice that the sky has changed while you were reading the names of streets. The world was always there, but certainty had made it quiet. The map in our pocket may still offer the fastest route, but the body remembers a slower, more articulate geography.

So I end with a modest defense of getting lost: not as a goal, not as nostalgia for hardship, and not as a rejection of technology, but as a defense of uncertainty itself. Let the blue dot guide us when a child needs a hospital, when weather is closing in, when the cost of delay is high. Let it speak plainly and save us from needless strain. But let us also leave some territory unclaimed, some routes unchosen, some afternoons without a destination. A map is a remarkable human invention, one of the great arguments made in lines and symbols about the shape of a world. It deserves our gratitude and our occasional disobedience. The map tells us where we are. Being lost, for a little while, lets us discover where we are.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
GENERIC_ESSAY — A polished, thesis-driven essay that develops a public argument through recurring images and a small number of personal details.

## Grounded reading
The voice is reflective and inviting, making a case for uncertainty without pretending that hardship is romantic. Its pathos comes from the contrast between efficient travel and the fuller attention of wandering: a detour brings smells, local voices, unfamiliar streets, and encounters with people into view. The essay asks the reader not to reject navigation technology, but to loosen the destination’s hold long enough to notice the world along the way.

## What the model chose to foreground
The essay foregrounds maps, the phone’s “blue dot,” walking, wrong turns, and local directions as ways of thinking about attention and control. It links getting lost to humility, human connection, belonging, and the limits of official borders and digital representations. The moral claim is measured: efficiency is useful, but should not become the only way we move through or understand the world.

## Evidence line
> Convenience was real, and I am grateful for it.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sustained imagery and repeated defense of uncertainty make the sample coherent and revealing, while its polished public-essay form makes the voice less individually distinctive.
